topics.title: A nomadic empire? Sources and the idea of 'barbarians'

learn.hook: Nomads are supposed to wander, not to build empires. Yet in the thirteenth century, herders from the Mongolian steppe built a state stretching from China to Europe.
points: 'Nomadic empire' sounds like a contradiction, since nomads are mobile and empires need settled control. The Mongols under Genghis Khan built a transcontinental empire across Asia and Europe in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

Most of our sources were written by city-based chroniclers, travellers and court historians in languages like Chinese, Persian, Arabic, Russian and Latin. Many were hostile to nomads and described them as destructive.

The word 'barbarian' comes from the Greek barbaros, meaning a non-Greek, whose speech sounded like meaningless babble to Greeks. Romans used it for Germanic tribes, Gauls and Huns; the Chinese had their own terms for steppe peoples.
Historians must read such sources critically: city-based writers often exaggerated nomads' violence and inflated casualty figures.

example.q: Why should a historian be cautious about a chronicler's claim that a Mongol attack killed over a million people in one city?
steps: Ask who wrote it: a city-based chronicler, often hostile to nomads.
Ask how the number was known: there were no census counts during sieges.
Consider purpose: dramatic figures emphasised the horror of the attack.
So the figure may be inflated, though the destruction was real.
example.answer: Because city-based writers were often biased against nomads and had no reliable way to count; such numbers may be exaggerated.

learn.reallife: News reports in India sometimes give very different crowd or casualty figures for the same event. Historians, like good journalists, ask who is counting and why.

topics.title: Genghis Khan's mandate and the fall of Bukhara

learn.hook: 'I am the punishment of God.' So, according to the chronicler Juwaini, Genghis Khan told the people of Bukhara in 1220.
points: Genghis Khan believed he had a mandate from Tengri, the Eternal Sky, to rule the world. This belief gave his conquests a sacred justification in Mongol eyes.
The Mongols' reach was immense: in 1236-1241 their armies moved through the Russian steppes into Poland and Hungary, reaching the outskirts of Vienna.

The Persian chronicler Juwaini described the capture of Bukhara in 1220. After the conquest, Genghis Khan gathered the rich residents at the festival ground and told them their great sins had brought God's punishment, in the form of himself, upon them.

Juwaini also quoted a survivor who escaped to Khurasan: 'They came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed.' Imagining how a resident of Bukhara felt hearing the speech is a classic way to read such a source.
Map work: the empire stretched from China and Korea in the east through Central Asia, Iran and Iraq to the Russian steppes and Eastern Europe.

example.q: Read Juwaini's survivor quote: 'They came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed.' What does it tell us, and what should we keep in mind?
steps: It describes rapid, destructive conquest: sieges, fire, killing, looting.
It comes from a victim, so it records real suffering.
Juwaini wrote as a Persian chronicler, so his framing reflects his viewpoint.
So it is powerful evidence of destruction, read with awareness of the author's perspective.
example.answer: It conveys the speed and violence of the conquest from a victim's view; historians also consider who recorded it and why.

learn.reallife: India's own chroniclers, from Kalhana's Rajatarangini to Persian court histories, also mixed vivid eyewitness accounts with their own viewpoints. Reading sources critically is a core history skill.

topics.title: Life on the steppe: pastoralists and hunter-gatherers

learn.hook: Long, harsh winters and short, dry summers: on the Mongolian steppe, farming barely worked, so people followed their animals across the grasslands.
points: The Mongols were diverse peoples linked by language to the Tatars, Khitan and Manchus to the east and Turkic tribes to the west. Some were pastoralists on the steppes of Central Asia (modern Mongolia); others were hunter-gatherers in the Siberian forests to the north.
Pastoralists raised horses, sheep and, to a lesser extent, goats and camels. They lived in felt tents called gers and moved seasonally between winter and summer pastures.
Hunter-gatherers lived north of the pastoralists, were poorer, and lived by trading furs from animals they trapped.
The harsh climate allowed agriculture only in limited seasons, and neither economy could support large populations, so no cities arose on the steppe.

Society was organised in patrilineal lineages; richer families were larger, owned more animals and pasture, and had many followers. Alliances and confederacies formed for defence or raids but were usually small and short-lived.

example.q: Why did no cities develop on the Mongolian steppe?
steps: The climate had harsh winters and short, dry summers.
Agriculture was possible only in limited seasons.
Herding and hunting could not support large, dense populations.
So people lived in small mobile groups, not cities.
example.answer: The harsh climate limited farming, so the economy could not support the large settled populations that cities need.

learn.reallife: Ladakh's Changpa herders move with yaks and pashmina goats across high pastures in seasonal cycles. Their tents and seasonal moves echo the Mongol gers on the steppe.

topics.title: The steppe and China: trade, raids and earlier confederacies

learn.hook: Horses and furs for grain and iron pots: the steppe and China needed each other. When trade broke down, raids began.
points: The steppe's limited resources pushed Mongols and other nomads to trade with their sedentary neighbour, China. Nomads exchanged horses, furs and game for agricultural produce and iron utensils.

Trade benefited both sides but could be tense. When trade broke down, nomads raided farming settlements. In response, China built fortifications: the Great Wall of China, begun from the third century BCE, partly to protect farmers from nomad raids.

Earlier steppe peoples formed large confederacies too: the Hsiung-nu, Juan-juan, Huns, Uighurs and Khitan. Attila the Hun (died 453) led a powerful confederacy in Europe, but his polity did not survive his death.
Genghis Khan's achievement was different: his empire outlived him and became a lasting transcontinental power.
Why trade mattered: the steppe could not provide grain, metal tools and luxuries, so trade (or raiding) was essential for nomad survival and for the Mongol elite's wealth.

example.q: Why was trade with China so important to the Mongols?
steps: The steppe could not produce enough grain.
Metal tools and utensils came from settled societies.
Nomads had surplus horses, furs and game to exchange.
So trade filled gaps in the steppe economy; when it failed, raids followed.
example.answer: Because the steppe lacked grain and iron goods, trade with China was essential; its breakdown led to raids.

learn.reallife: India's border haats with Bangladesh let people across the border exchange local produce peacefully. Exchange across ecological and political boundaries reduces conflict, a lesson the steppe-China frontier teaches too.

learn.hook: A boy whose father was murdered, who was once captured and enslaved, grew up to be called the 'Universal Ruler'. This is Temujin's story.
points: Genghis Khan was born around 1162 near the Onon river in northern Mongolia and named Temujin. His father Yesugei was the chieftain of the Kiyat, a family of the Borjigid clan.

His father was assassinated when he was young, and his mother Oelun-eke raised Temujin, his brothers and step-brothers in hardship. Temujin was captured and enslaved in the 1170s, and his wife Borte was kidnapped soon after marriage.
He built alliances: Boghurchu became his first friend and ally; Jamuqa became his blood-brother (anda); and Ong Khan, ruler of the Kereyits, was an old ally of his father.

Jamuqa later became a rival and was defeated. Temujin then moved against the Tatars (his father's assassins), the Kereyits and Ong Khan (1203). The defeat of the Naiman people and Jamuqa in 1206 left him dominant.
At a quriltai (assembly of Mongol chiefs) in 1206, he was proclaimed Genghis Khan, the 'Oceanic Khan' or 'Universal Ruler'.

example.q: Trace how alliances and conflicts helped Temujin rise to power.
steps: Early alliances: Boghurchu, Jamuqa (anda) and Ong Khan gave him support.
He used these to defeat rivals, including Jamuqa when he turned against him.
He took on the Tatars, the Kereyits and Ong Khan.
Defeating the Naiman and Jamuqa made him dominant; the quriltai of 1206 confirmed him as Genghis Khan.
example.answer: He used alliances to build strength, then defeated rivals one by one until the 1206 quriltai proclaimed him Genghis Khan.

learn.reallife: Start-up founders often begin with a few loyal partners, then grow by alliances and competition. Temujin's rise shows how networks of trust can build power from nothing.

topics.title: Campaigns in China and Central Asia

learn.hook: One rash decision by a sultan, executing Mongol envoys at Otrar, brought Genghis Khan's armies crashing into the cities of Central Asia.
points: After 1206, Genghis Khan first turned to China, then divided into three kingdoms: the Hsi Hsia of the northwest, the Chin (Jurchen) dynasty in the north, and the Sung in the south.
The Hsi Hsia were defeated, and the Chin were attacked; Peking (Beijing) was sacked in 1215 after a long siege.

In 1218 the Sultan of Khwarazm, Muhammad, executed Mongol envoys (the Otrar incident). In the campaign of 1219-1221, great cities such as Otrar, Bukhara, Samarqand, Balkh, Gurganj, Merv, Nishapur and Herat surrendered or were sacked.

At Nishapur, after a Mongol prince (Genghis Khan's son-in-law) was killed, the Mongols ordered savage reprisals. Mongol forces pursued the Sultan and his son Jalaluddin; Genghis Khan abandoned a campaign along the Indus and returned to Mongolia.
Genghis Khan died in 1227, having created a vast empire across China, Central Asia and parts of Iran.

topics.title: How the Mongols fought and how chroniclers counted

learn.hook: Mongol armies used frozen rivers as highways in winter. Few enemies expected an attack in the coldest months.
points: Mongol success rested on horsemanship and archery: mounted archers moved fast and shot accurately from horseback, using light equipment.
Speed and mobility let armies cover vast distances; they also campaigned in winter, using frozen rivers as highways into enemy territory.
From campaigns in China, the Mongols learnt to use siege engines and naphtha bombardment against walled cities.

Chroniclers gave enormous figures for those killed, for example more than a million at single cities like Nishapur and Herat. These numbers were exaggerated estimates: no one could count precisely, and writers sought to convey horror.
Historians accept that destruction was real and severe, including damage to irrigation systems, but read the statistics as rhetoric rather than exact data.

example.q: A chronicle says over 1.7 million people died at Nishapur. Give two reasons to doubt the exact figure.
steps: Medieval cities rarely had populations that large.
There was no reliable counting during or after a massacre.
Writers often inflated numbers to stress horror and moral lessons.
So the figure signals great destruction, not a precise count.
example.answer: Population sizes and counting methods make it unlikely; such figures were rhetorical exaggerations of real destruction.

learn.reallife: Indian Army mountain units train for winter operations in Siachen and Ladakh. Mobility, light equipment and mastery of harsh terrain still decide campaigns, as they did for the Mongols.

learn.hook: Genghis Khan died in 1227, but the empire kept growing: Russia, Baghdad and finally all of China fell to his heirs.
points: Mongol expansion after Genghis Khan came in two phases: 1236-1242, into the Russian steppes, Bulghar, Kiev, Poland and Hungary; and 1255-1300, the conquest of all of China, Iran, Iraq and Syria.
Great Khans after Genghis Khan included Ogodei, Guyuk and Mongke. Batu, grandson of Genghis Khan through Jochi, led the campaigns in Russia.
Hulegu, a grandson through Toluy, founded the Il-Khanid state in Iran and captured Baghdad in 1258.
Western expansion was halted by the defeat of Mongol forces by the Mamluks of Egypt in 1260 and by internal Mongol politics (rivalries among Genghis Khan's descendants).
Qubilai Khan completed the conquest of China (the Sung) by 1279 and ruled as founder of the Yuan dynasty. Silk Route cities such as Samarqand, Bukhara and Kashgar linked the Mongol world.

topics.title: A new army and the four ulus

learn.hook: Genghis Khan deliberately broke up old tribes and mixed their men into new units. Loyalty to him replaced loyalty to clan.
points: Mongol and other nomad men were organised into a decimal army: units of 10, 100, 1,000 and roughly 10,000 soldiers (tumen). This followed an old steppe tradition.
Genghis Khan broke up old tribal groupings and distributed their members into new military units. A soldier who tried to move away without permission was severely punished.

Those who had served him loyally for years were given the title noyan, commanders of the new army. Old relationships such as anda (blood-brother) and naukar (bondsman or companion) bound followers to him.

Conquered territories were divided among his four sons into ulus (shares of dominion): Jochi, Chaghatai, Ogodei and Toluy. Ogodei was named Great Khan; Toluy, the youngest, received the Mongol homeland.
Why restructure? Old tribal loyalties caused feuds and weak, short-lived confederacies. New mixed units created loyalty to Genghis Khan and his family, turning many tribes into one disciplined army.

topics.title: The yam, the paiza and the Pax Mongolica

learn.hook: Fresh horses waiting at relay posts across thousands of kilometres: the Mongol yam carried messages faster than anything else in its time.
points: The yam was a courier system: fresh mounts and despatch riders were placed at outposts at fixed distances, giving fast communication across the empire. It was financed by a levy (qubcur) paid by Mongol nomads from their herds.
Travellers received a passport or safe-conduct pass, called paiza in Persian and gerege in Mongolian. Merchants paid a tax called baj for the same right.
Under Mongol rule, trade along the Silk Route reached its peak, with goods, ideas and people moving safely across Asia. This security is called the Pax Mongolica (Mongol peace).
Travellers like William of Rubruck, sent by Louis IX of France to the Great Khan Mongke's court (1254), described its diversity: people of many faiths and lands at the court.
The Pax Mongolica was built on conquest and control, yet it linked China, Central Asia, Iran and Europe as never before.

example.q: How did the yam help the Mongols rule a vast empire?
steps: Messages had to cross thousands of kilometres.
Relay stations provided fresh horses and riders at fixed distances.
Information moved quickly between the Great Khan and his commanders.
So the empire could be controlled and coordinated despite its size.
example.answer: By providing fast, reliable communication across the empire through relay posts with fresh horses.

learn.reallife: India Post's network of over 1.5 lakh post offices and the Indian Railways' mail services are modern 'yams', and the dak chowki relay system of Indian sultanates worked the same way.

topics.title: Ruling settled peoples: administrators, peasants and Ghazan Khan

learn.hook: Herders want pasture; peasants want fields. Ruling Persia and China forced the Mongols to choose which mattered more.
points: Conquerors needed administrators, so the Mongols recruited civil officials from conquered peoples: Chinese, Persians, Uighurs and others.

Yeh-lu Ch'u-ts'ai, a Chinese adviser to Ogodei, persuaded him that taxing peasants was more profitable than turning farmland into pasture. The Juwaini family of Persian administrators served the Mongols, and Rashiduddin was wazir to the Il-Khan Ghazan.

Ghazan Khan (Il-Khan, 1295-1304), a convert to Islam, gave a speech (drafted by Rashiduddin) urging Mongol commanders not to harass the peasantry, because ruined peasants could not pay taxes or feed the army.
There was tension between nomadic and sedentary interests: nomads wanted pasture and booty; peasants needed stability. Over time, many Mongols in conquered lands became more settled.

Comparison: like the Mongols, the Bedouins of Arabia were pastoral nomads who built a large state once united; but the Bedouins were united by Islam, while the Mongols were united by Genghis Khan's leadership, military organisation and the yasa.

example.q: Why did Ghazan Khan urge his commanders not to harass peasants?
steps: Peasants produced the crops that fed the army and paid taxes.
If harassed, they would flee or stop farming.
Then the state would lose revenue and food.
So protecting peasants protected the state's stability and prosperity.
example.answer: Because the state's revenue and food depended on peasants; harassing them would ruin the economy.

topics.title: The yasa: from decree to legal code

learn.hook: A word that meant 'order' slowly became the name of a sacred legal code, and was still being invoked by rulers in Bukhara about four centuries after Genghis Khan.
points: At the quriltai of 1206, Genghis Khan's laws were associated with the term yasaq, which originally meant law, decree or order. The few details we know concern administration: the hunt, the army and the postal system.
By the mid-thirteenth century, the Mongols used the related term yasa to mean the legal code believed to have been formulated by Genghis Khan.
The yasa gave the Mongols a shared identity and confidence; it showed their loyalty to Genghis Khan's traditions and gave them legitimacy and authority over sedentary subjects.

Its meaning kept changing. In the sixteenth century, the Uzbek ruler 'Abdullah Khan of Bukhara was described as performing Muslim festival prayers in a way the writer called 'according to the yasa of Genghis Khan', showing how later rulers reinterpreted it.
So over about four centuries, yasa shifted from a set of specific orders to a respected code and then to a symbol of Genghisid tradition and legitimacy.

example.q: Trace how the meaning of 'yasa' changed over four centuries.
steps: Originally (yasaq): a law, decree or order, mainly on administration.
Mid-thirteenth century: the legal code believed to come from Genghis Khan.
It gave Mongols identity and legitimacy over subjects.
Sixteenth century: invoked by an Uzbek ruler in Bukhara for practices linked to Islam, i.e. a symbol of Genghisid tradition.
example.answer: From a decree, to Genghis Khan's legal code, to a symbol of legitimacy reinterpreted by later rulers.

learn.reallife: In India, the Constitution's words are reinterpreted by the Supreme Court over time; 'right to life' under Article 21 now includes privacy and a clean environment. Like the yasa, a founding text can grow in meaning.

topics.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongols in world history

learn.hook: In Persian and Chinese chronicles he is a destroyer. In Mongolia today, his face is on banknotes and his statue towers over the steppe. Same man, two images.
points: Chronicles of conquered city-dwellers portray Genghis Khan as a conqueror and destroyer of cities responsible for vast killing. In modern Mongolia he is honoured as the great national hero who united the Mongols.
Mongol rule was multi-ethnic, multi-lingual and multi-religious: it included Chinese, Persians, Turks, Russians and others, and employed people of many faiths.
After decades of Soviet influence, Mongolia in the 1990s revived Genghis Khan as a symbol of national identity and pride.

Later rulers drew on his legacy. Timur, who was not a direct descendant, married a Genghisid princess and called himself guregen (royal son-in-law). The Mughal emperor Babur descended from Genghis Khan on his mother's side and from Timur on his father's side. Uzbek khans also claimed Genghisid descent.

Timeline: Temujin born c. 1162; Genghis Khan 1206; death 1227; Baghdad 1258; Mamluk defeat 1260; China conquered 1279; Ghazan Khan 1295-1304; much later, Mongolia's revolution of 1921 and modern republic.

example.q: Why do chroniclers and modern Mongolians remember Genghis Khan so differently?
steps: Chroniclers were city-dwellers of conquered lands who suffered the conquests.
They stressed destruction and killing.
Modern Mongolians see him as the founder of their nation who united the tribes.
So memory depends on who is remembering and why.
example.answer: Because conquered city-based writers recorded his violence, while Mongolians remember him as their unifier and national hero.

learn.reallife: The Mughals proudly traced descent from Timur and Genghis Khan. Babur's memoir, the Baburnama, shows how this lineage shaped the rulers who came to India in 1526.
